In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: libiscsi: Reject a negative task index from parse_pdu_itt  A transport that implements parse_pdu_itt hands libiscsi an index taken from the PDU, and both lookups bound it from above only:        if (i >= session->cmds_max)  i and cmds_max are both int, so a negative index passes and session->cmds[i] is read from before the array.  be2iscsi produces one. beiscsi_parse_pdu() assigns the raw tag,        *index = (int)itt;  and beiscsi_complete_pdu() forwards an unsolicited NOP-In from the hardware async ring without replacing its ITT, so the value is the target's. It also reports the session's own age rather than the one in the tag, which leaves the age comparison in iscsi_verify_itt() with nothing to reject.  Bound the index from below in both lookups.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: xen/scsifront: Check for a NULL shadow entry on a backend response  scsifront_do_response() validates the rqid in a backend response against VSCSIIF_MAX_REQS before using it to index info->shadow[], but then dereferences the entry to test ->inflight without checking that the slot is populated.  Shadow slots are NULL before a command is submitted (the host private area is zeroed at allocation) and are reset to NULL in _scsifront_put_rqid() once a request completes, so an in-range rqid that does not correspond to an outstanding request makes the frontend dereference a NULL pointer.  A malicious or buggy backend can thus crash the guest by returning a response whose rqid is in range but not in flight -- for example a spurious response before any command has been issued, or a duplicate of one already completed.  The ring has only VSCSIIF_MAX_REQS (16) slots, so before the first command every in-range rqid selects a NULL slot.  Reject a response whose shadow slot is not populated.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: st: Fix use-after-free race between st_remove() and st_open()  st_remove() drops the probe reference on the scsi_tape with kref_put() and only afterwards removes its index from st_index_idr. If that was the last reference, scsi_tape_release() frees the structure while it is still published in the idr.  scsi_tape_get(), called from st_open(), looks up the tape in st_index_idr and takes a reference under st_ref_mutex and st_index_lock. remove_cdevs() does not wait for opens that are already past chrdev_open(), so an open that is blocked on st_ref_mutex while st_remove() holds it can take the mutex as soon as st_remove() drops it, find the freed tpnt in the idr and call kref_get() on it:    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in st_open   Write of size 4 ...    st_open (drivers/scsi/st.c:254 drivers/scsi/st.c:1291)    chrdev_open   ...   Freed by task ...:    kfree    st_remove (drivers/scsi/st.c:4512)  Remove the index from the idr before dropping the reference, all under st_ref_mutex. A concurrent scsi_tape_get() now either runs first and holds a valid reference that keeps the tape alive, or runs afterwards and finds nothing, so st_open() fails with -ENXIO.  This restores the ordering st_remove() had before the conversion to st_index_idr, where the tape was unpublished from scsi_tapes[] before the final kref_put().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: bsg: Pass reply_len to bsg_setup_queue() to fit UFS ARPMB replies  bsg-lib allocates a 96-byte (SCSI_SENSE_BUFFERSIZE) reply buffer per job, but struct ufs_rpmb_reply is 104 bytes: a 40-byte struct ufs_bsg_reply followed by a 64-byte EHS. When an Advanced RPMB command returns an EHS, ufshcd_advanced_rpmb_req_handler() copies it right after the 40-byte header and writes 8 bytes past the end of the buffer.  Let each BSG transport pass its reply buffer size to bsg_setup_queue() and have ufs_bsg request sizeof(struct ufs_rpmb_reply), so the full reply reaches user space. Other transports keep SCSI_SENSE_BUFFERSIZE.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ring-buffer: Fix false warning in ring_buffer_map_get_reader()  The mmap reader can warn when it catches up with a writer that is still committing events. rb_get_reader_page() returns NULL in this case, but ring_buffer_map_get_reader() treats that result as an error.  The initial rb_per_cpu_empty() check filters out an empty buffer, but it does not guarantee that the next reader page has committed data. Writers do not take reader_lock and can advance commit_page before publishing the committed length on the new page. rb_get_reader_page() can swap to that page, catch up with the writer and return NULL.  Handle NULL through the existing no-data exit without warning. Remove the caller's reader_page == commit_page check as well, since the reader-page helper already handles that case. The existing metadata update and return path remain in place.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ring-buffer: Fix the sub-buffer array base in rb_meta_subbuf_idx()  On a persistent ring buffer, rb_meta_subbuf_idx() can return an index one sub-buffer too high.  rb_setup_ids_meta_page() then fills subbuf_ids[] shifted by one and leaves subbuf_ids[0] NULL, which __rb_map_vma() dereferences when userspace maps trace_pipe_raw.  rb_update_meta_reader() writes two such indices into meta->buffers[], which rb_cpu_meta_valid() would reject on the next boot, discarding the previous boot's trace.  A CPU's sub-buffer array starts after its meta header and the nr_subbufs integers that follow, aligned up to a sub-buffer.  rb_meta_subbuf_idx() inverts that calculation but skips only the integers, not the header, so its base is one sub-buffer low whenever the omitted header size crosses the alignment boundary.  Invert the calculation with rb_subbufs_from_meta() rather than repeating it.  rb_range_buffer() maps an index back to an address through the same helper, so the two directions can no longer disagree.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ring-buffer: Do not show buffer_meta for CPUs without a buffer  The per_cpu/cpuN/buffer_meta files are created for every possible CPU, but buffer->buffers[cpu] is only allocated once that CPU comes online. Reading the file of a CPU that never came online dereferences a NULL cpu_buffer in rbm_start().  Fail the open with -ENODEV when the CPU has no buffer, as the other per CPU ring buffer interfaces do.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  i2c: viai2c-wmt: Fix clock leak in wmt_i2c_probe()  In wmt_i2c_probe(), i2c->clk is acquired using of_clk_get(). If any subsequent operation fails or when the module is unloaded, the clock reference count is never decremented via clk_put(), leading to a resource leak.  Switch to devm_clk_get() so that the clock is automatically managed and released.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  gpio: shared: fix use-after-free bug when adding shared proxies  The GPIO lookup table can stay alive for longer than the kobject whose name string's address we're assigning to lookup->dev_id. Fix a potential UAF by duplicating the string.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  tracing/histograms: Reject non-stacktrace fields for synthetic stacktrace fields  In check_synth_field(), when a synthetic event field is a stacktrace (field->is_stack) and the histogram field is not a "long[" stacktrace array, validation falls through to the generic size and signedness comparison.  Because parse_synth_field() sets a stacktrace field's type to "__data_loc unsigned long[]", its size is sizeof(u64) and synth_field_signed() marks it as signed.  Consequently, any 8-byte signed scalar histogram field passes the fallback check, and its scalar value is subsequently dereferenced as a kernel stacktrace pointer in get_field_size() and trace_stack().  Furthermore, checking strstr(hist_field->type, "long[") is insufficient because tracepoint fields defined with __bitmask() or __rel_bitmask() also have type "__data_loc unsigned long[]" or "__rel_loc unsigned long[]", whilst create_hist_field() treats them as 4-byte scalar values without HIST_FIELD_FL_STACKTRACE.  Propagate HIST_FIELD_FL_STACKTRACE to variable references and field variables (whilst excluding variable aliases from per-element stacktrace capture), and reject any mismatch between HIST_FIELD_FL_STACKTRACE and field->is_stack in check_synth_field().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  spi: imx: fix slab corruption from undersized DMA bounce buffers  Since commit faa8e404ad8e ("spi: imx: support dynamic burst length for ECSPI DMA mode"), the driver allocates its private DMA TX/RX buffers with kzalloc(dma_len), where dma_len is only rounded up to 4 bytes, but maps, syncs and unmaps them with DMA_CACHE_ALIGNED_LEN(dma_len), i.e. rounded up to the cache line size. As a result, the DMA API operates on memory beyond the end of the allocation.  This was observed on a custom i.MX8MP platform with an mcp251xfd CAN controller under heavy RPMSG load, as a series of refcount_t warnings triggered from rpmsg_recv_done() in virtio_rpmsg_bus:    refcount_t: addition on 0; use-after-free.   refcount_t: underflow; use-after-free.   refcount_t: saturated; leaking memory.  Leading finally to an "Unable to handle kernel paging request" oops. Reproducing this problem took between 30 minutes and roughly 30 hours under the same workload.  Hardware watchpoints on the refcount of a struct rpmsg_endpoint showed it was overwritten from 2 to 1 by __pi_memcpy_generic() in the irq/155-spi2.0 thread. Additionally it was found that a "normal" rpmsg_recv_done() took 11µs +/-2µs from its kref_get to kref_put. In the error case the same sequence took about 215µs +/-10µs. Based on this, an LLM was used to identify the size mismatch fixed here.  Allocate the buffers with DMA_CACHE_ALIGNED_LEN(dma_len) so they cover the full mapped length, and use the same length for dma_sync_single_for_cpu() to stay consistent with map and unmap.  With this patch applied, the same workload ran for more than 200 hours without the problem reproducing.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  sctp: revalidate output stream after association connect wait  When message interleaving is enabled, the first send waits for association establishment before building its data chunks.  The wait drops the socket lock, and handshake processing can reduce the output stream count to the peer-advertised inbound stream count.  sctp_stream_init() then frees the extension of every removed stream.  The sender resumes with the stream that it checked before the wait.  If the peer removed that stream, sctp_outq_tail() later dereferences its NULL extension.  Fatal-oops policies then panic the host.  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x38-0x3f] RIP: sctp_outq_tail+0x49e/0xaa0 Call Trace:  sctp_primitive_SEND  sctp_sendmsg_to_asoc  sctp_sendmsg  A range check alone is insufficient.  Stream reconfiguration can grow the output count again while the lock is released without recreating extensions freed by the earlier shrink.  The stream can then be in range while its extension remains NULL.  The send-buffer wait has the same issue.  Factor the range and extension checks into a helper and repeat both after each send-path wait that drops the socket lock.  Once the lock is reacquired, the validation remains stable through data creation and queueing.  If validation fails after the connect wait, the auto-created association is already established.  Return ESRCH so the existing caller path keeps it under state-machine ownership instead of freeing it directly, which would leave protocol, counter and socket state inconsistent.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: rds: fix uninitialized trans dereference in CM event handler  rds_rdma_cm_event_handler_cmn() assigns trans only when the RDMA device is an InfiniBand CA (RDMA_NODE_IB_CA).  On any other device type, e.g. an iWARP RNIC such as siw, trans stays uninitialized, but the event switch dereferences it: unconditionally in the RDMA_CM_EVENT_CONNECT_REQUEST case via trans->cm_handle_connect(), and (with a connection context) in the ROUTE_RESOLVED and ESTABLISHED cases.  An RDS listener on an iWARP device therefore crashes the kernel as soon as a connect request arrives: with CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO the wild load becomes a NULL dereference at offset 0xa0 (&trans->cm_handle_connect) in the iw_cm_wq workqueue.  GCC masks the bug in default builds by folding the uninitialized load into &rds_ib_transport; Clang-built kernels take the real uninitialized path and oops.  The active side can land on a non-IB device too: the id that rds_ib_conn_path_connect() creates is not restricted to a node type, so rdma_resolve_addr() binds it to whichever device serves the local address, and an iWARP RNIC on the same netdev qualifies.  The crash there is different: resolving a route on an iWARP id never fills in cm_id->route.path_rec, and the ROUTE_RESOLVED case writes path_rec[0].sl before it calls into the transport.  The iWARP transport was dropped long ago and IB is the only transport left, so make that explicit: initialize trans to &rds_ib_transport at declaration, drop the conditional assignment, reject a connect request that arrives on a non-IB device, and drop a connection whose address resolved to one instead of resolving a route on it.  The rejection is limited to RDMA_CM_EVENT_CONNECT_REQUEST on purpose: a non-zero return from the handler makes rdma_cm destroy the id the event was delivered on, which is right for the request's freshly created id but would free a connection id that RDS still owns for any other event.  On the active side the id stays ic->i_cm_id and the connection's shutdown destroys it, so that case returns 0.  [achender: reject only on RDMA_CM_EVENT_CONNECT_REQUEST instead of  bailing out for every event on a non-IB device, so that rdma_cm does  not destroy connection ids RDS still tracks; drop a connection whose  address resolved to a non-IB device before a route is resolved on it;  changelog adjusted]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net/sched: fix use-after-free in __tcf_action_put()  __tcf_action_put() decrements the reference count before decrementing the binding count. Another thread can free the action between these operations, causing the binding-count update to access freed memory. KASAN reports it as:    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in __tcf_action_put+0x327/0x340   Write of size 4 at addr ff11000000d46420 by task tc-put-pause/64  Hold the action IDR mutex across both counter updates and IDR removal, keeping cleanup outside the lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  mshv_vtl: Check per-CPU register page before mmap  Register-page setup is optional for each CPU. If allocation or registration fails, mshv_vtl_configure_reg_page() warns and leaves that CPU's reg_page NULL, but initial context setup continues successfully. Meanwhile, successful setup on another CPU sets the global mshv_has_reg_page flag.  mshv_vtl_fault() checks this global flag before selecting the requested CPU's register page. With mixed setup results across online CPUs, the check passes even for a CPU with no register page, reaching get_page(NULL) when userspace faults in that mapping.  Check the selected per-CPU register page before taking its reference and return VM_FAULT_SIGBUS if it is absent.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  futex: Fix mm reuse handling for FUT_OFF_MMSHARED  A FUT_OFF_MMSHARED futex is a shared futex that refers to an MM. It is possible for a process to wait on a shared futex with a different MM because a FUT_OFF_INODE waiter can be requeued onto a FUT_OFF_MMSHARED futex by another process. This can cause FUT_OFF_MMSHARED waiters on a freed MM to consume wakeups intended for a newly allocated MM at the same address.  Fix it by keying FUT_OFF_MMSHARED using a unique 64-bit per-MM ID. Leave private futexes as before to avoid influencing the performance of the hotpath.  (Multi-threaded processes typically implicitly use FUT_OFF_MMSHARED by setting clear_child_tid such that it points into anonymous memory, which causes mm_release() in a multi-threaded mm to perform FUTEX_WAKE.)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  namespace: a mount that copy_tree() leaves out can't take over a lock  Since commit c62a4766937e ("move_mount: transfer MNT_LOCKED") a mount can be moved beneath a locked mount. The lock moves from the old cover to the new mount which takes over the job of hiding what's under it and the old cover can be unmounted. That works as long as the new mount stays. But the caller picks the new mount and copy_tree() leaves a mount of a mount namespace file out of every copy made without CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE, together with everything mounted on it, and never looks at MNT_LOCKED. unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) and mount propagation make such copies.  So a task that is root in its own user namespace gets rid of a locked cover on a file without a race and without touching the filesystem below it. It makes a child with a mount namespace of its own, binds the child's /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt beneath the cover with MOVE_MOUNT_BENEATH, which hands the lock to that bind, and calls unshare(CLONE_NEWNS). The new mount namespace has nothing on the file. That's the usual way to mask a single file, a bind of /dev/null or of an empty file. With a bind of an ordinary file the file stays covered.  copy_tree() already refuses to leave out a locked unbindable mount with -EPERM since commit df7342b24018 ("mount: Don't allow copying MNT_UNBINDABLE|MNT_LOCKED mounts"). Do the same for a locked mount of a mount namespace file. That also covers a tree copied with CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE and attached into a mount namespace of another user namespace where lock_mnt_tree() locks it. Note that unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) and clone(CLONE_NEWNS) fail with EPERM from such a mount namespace from then on. The mount can't be left out and it can't be unmounted.  And refuse to move a mount of a mount namespace file beneath a locked mount in the first place. Otherwise the task ends up with a mount it can't unmount and an unshare() that fails for good.  Chris also found a second mount that goes away by itself, a clone of an automounted mount that shrink_submounts() took along with its parent. Commit f78ddcc87224 ("namespace: never expire a locked mount") took care of that one.  Chris's reproducer is appended. Mode nsfile reads SECRET after the unshare() on 7.3-rc7, with this patch the move_mount() fails with EINVAL and the file stays covered. nsfile-control uses an ordinary file and reads MASK both ways.    // SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0   /*    * Get rid of a locked cover with MOVE_MOUNT_BENEATH.    *    * The "admin" (root) makes a tmpfs W:    *     W/D         file, holds SECRET, covered by a bind of a file with MASK    *     W/Dd/inner  file, holds SECRET, Dd is covered by a bind of a directory    *                 whose "inner" holds MASK    *     W/own       directory of uid 1000 with the file "mine" and the    *                 directory "minedir", whose "inner" holds MINE    *     W/dbg       debugfs, mode 755. dbg/tracing is an automount point    * The "attacker" is uid 1000. It enters a new user namespace with a new mount    * namespace, so W and both covers are locked there.    *    * usage: prog MODE    *   plain      put a bind of own/mine beneath the cover of D, unmount the cover    *   nsfile     put a bind of the mount namespace file of a child beneath the    *              cover of D, then unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)    *   nsfile-control    the same with a bind of own/mine    *   shrink     put a bind of the automounted tracefs beneath the cover of Dd,    *              unmount the cover, put a tmpfs beneath W, call umount(W), which fails    *   shrink-control    the same with a bind of own/minedir    * The environment variable AUTOMOUNT_DIR names another automount point for "shrink".    */   #define _GNU_SOURCE   #include <errno.h>   #include <fcntl.h>   #include <grp.h>   #include <sched.h>   #include <signal.h>   #include <stdio.h>   #include <stdlib.h>   #include <string.h>   #include <unistd.h>   ---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ntfs3: free the sbi after a grace period  If the "nocase" mount option ntfs3 uses custom hash and dentry compare functions. Both access ntfs3 superblock private information in rcu pathwalk. ntfs_put_super() and ntfs3_kill_sb() drop the info without any rcu delay. A lookup that's still inside the filesystem when the last reference to the mount is dropped causes a UAF. With a pathwalk held up in ntfs_d_hash() while the last reference to the mount goes away:    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ntfs_nls_to_utf16+0x752/0x940   Read of size 8 at addr ff1100010453c850 by task walker/99   Call Trace:    <TASK>    ntfs_nls_to_utf16+0x752/0x940    ntfs_d_hash+0x22b/0x500    link_path_walk+0x11ad/0x1d30    path_lookupat+0x63/0xb00    filename_lookup+0x1f1/0x5b0    vfs_statx+0xd7/0x3b0   [...]   Allocated by task 95:    __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x249/0x560    ntfs_init_fs_context+0x2db/0x5a0    alloc_fs_context+0x52e/0xc70   [...]   Freed by task 98:    kfree+0x1db/0x5b0    deactivate_locked_super+0x9c/0xf0    cleanup_mnt+0x9f/0x130    task_work_run+0x131/0x250  The bug is currently masked by the grace period in namespace_unlock() for umount(2). Keep the necessary information until the filesystem private info is freed and free it with an rcu delay.  ntfs3_free_sbi() now runs from an rcu callback and drops the upcase table via ntfs_put_shared(). So switch s_shared_lock over to spin_lock_bh(). Otherwise the callback can deadlock against a task holding the lock on the same cpu.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ipc: drop the mqueue mount with kern_unmount() on setup failure  mq_init_ns() creates the mqueue mount with fc_mount_longterm(), so its ->mnt_ns is MNT_NS_INTERNAL. When setting up the mqueue or ipc sysctls or msg_init_ns() fails afterwards, create_ipc_ns() drops it with a plain mntput(). With ->mnt_ns set that takes the fast path of mntput_no_expire(). The count drops to zero and nothing ever kills the mount, so the mount and the mqueue superblock are leaked.  Commit dc55e35f9e81 ("ipc: Store mqueue sysctls in the ipc namespace") added the first failure path after mq_init_ns() and never dropped the mount. Commit 7229d74e5e8c ("ipc: create_ipc_ns: drop mqueue mount on sysctl setup failure") tried to fix that with a mntput() but that doesn't help for a long-term mount.  Use kern_unmount(). free_ipc() open-codes the same thing for a namespace that made it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  eventfs: Free the eventfs_inode after an rcu grace period too  tracefs_d_revalidate() reads ->is_freed of the eventfs_inode that dentry->d_fsdata points to, and ->d_revalidate() is called in rcu pathwalk mode with nothing but rcu_read_lock() held. The dentry itself stays around for such a walker, but tracefs_d_release() drops its reference to the eventfs_inode when the dentry is killed, and release_ei() then frees it after a grace period of eventfs_srcu. An SRCU grace period doesn't wait for rcu_read_lock() sections, so the walker can read an eventfs_inode that is already gone.  With a pathwalk held up in tracefs_d_revalidate() while the dentry goes away:    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in tracefs_d_revalidate+0x76/0x90   Read of size 1 at addr ff1100010152d8d0 by task walker/97   Call Trace:    <TASK>    tracefs_d_revalidate+0x76/0x90    lookup_fast+0x320/0x640    path_lookupat+0x160/0xb00    filename_lookup+0x1f1/0x5b0    vfs_statx+0xd7/0x3b0    vfs_fstatat+0x4d/0x90    __do_sys_newfstatat+0xa0/0x100    do_syscall_64+0x10e/0x5e0    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f   [...]   Allocated by task 1:    __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x249/0x560    eventfs_create_dir+0x7a/0x590    event_create_dir+0x2fb/0xcf0    trace_add_event_call+0xbf/0x150   [...]   Freed by task 11:    kfree+0x1db/0x5b0    srcu_invoke_callbacks+0x3a3/0x620    process_one_work+0x937/0x1810    worker_thread+0x4f1/0xd60  Before commit 8e556432477e ("eventfs: Use SRCU for freeing eventfs_inodes") release_ei() used call_rcu(), which covered the walker, while eventfs_iterate() needs the SRCU grace period. Wait for both and chain call_rcu() from the SRCU callback.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ext4: free the sbi after a grace period  ext4_get_link() follows a symlink that keeps its target in a data block in rcu pathwalk mode with ext4_getblk(EXT4_GET_BLOCKS_CACHED_NOWAIT). That reads s_mount_state in the ASSERT() of ext4_getblk() and again in ext4_es_lookup_extent(), and the lookup bumps the extent status hit or miss counter, all through sb->s_fs_info.  ext4_put_super() destroys those counters, clears sb->s_fs_info and frees the sbi without waiting for a grace period. A pathwalk that is still in ext4_get_link() when the last reference to the mount goes away then dereferences a NULL s_fs_info, the freed sbi or the destroyed percpu counters.  With a pathwalk held up in ext4_get_link() while the last reference goes away:    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x00000000000000a8-0x00000000000000af]   RIP: 0010:ext4_getblk+0xf0/0x640   Call Trace:    <TASK>    ext4_get_link+0x26c/0x410    pick_link+0xf96/0x1780    step_into_slowpath+0x9b8/0x1250    path_lookupat+0x484/0xb00    filename_lookup+0x1f1/0x5b0    vfs_statx+0xd7/0x3b0    vfs_fstatat+0x4d/0x90    __do_sys_newfstatat+0xa0/0x100    do_syscall_64+0x10e/0x5e0    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f  So far that has been hard to hit. umount(2) waits for a grace period in namespace_unlock() before it drops the mount, so only a mount whose last reference goes away elsewhere, like the close of a file or a chdir out of a lazily unmounted directory, can race a walker.  Keep sb->s_fs_info and free the sbi together with the extent status counters after a grace period. Split the counters out of ext4_es_unregister_shrinker() for that. The shrinker still gets wasted in ext4_put_super(), the counters go with the sbi.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  fsnotify: prevent mark additions during connector teardown  fsnotify_destroy_marks() keeps a reference to its current mark while it drops conn->lock to destroy the mark. This stabilizes the forward-walk cursor, but does not prevent a new mark from being inserted before it. For example, an inotify watch re-added after IN_IGNORED sorts before the old, detached mark for the same group. The walk can miss the replacement and then detach the entire connector from the object.  The replacement is still on its group's marks_list and, for inotify, in the watch IDR. The group mutex no longer protects the connector's object from disappearing. An unprivileged fdinfo read racing the final detach can consequently call igrab(NULL):    BUG: KASAN: null-ptr-deref in igrab+0x24/0x100   Write of size 4 at addr 0000000000000148   Call Trace:    igrab+0x24/0x100    inotify_show_fdinfo+0x1dc/0x5e0    seq_show+0x397/0x690  Set a DESTROYING flag under conn->lock before starting the walk, and reject new marks on that connector with -ENOENT. The existing add-mark error paths undo the temporary group-list entry and the backend's watch allocation. Do not wait for teardown while holding the group mutex, which the destroyer needs. Once the old connector is detached, an add can install a fresh connector as before.  This closes the insertion race for all object types using the common connector teardown, without changing the mark reference or SRCU lifetime rules.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  KVM: nVMX: Reset MMU back to the root MMU if loading L2 state fails for !VM-Entry  Reset the vCPU's MMU pointer back to the root MMU if loading L2 state fails in the "not from VM-Entry" case, i.e. when emulating RSM or handling KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE.  Failure to unwind the MMU pointer results in KVM trying to run L1 with a nested MMU, and is especially problematic if the vCPU manages to free its nested state before the VM crashes.  Constructing the root for a nested EPT MMU goes through vmcs12, which is dynamically allocated/freed when nVMX is enabled/disabled.  And so if the nested state is freed with the MMU still pointing at the nested MMU, KVM will hit a NULL pointer deref when attempting to get L1=>L2 EPTP.    BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000078   #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode   #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page   PGD 114a2d067 P4D 111743067 PUD 11141f067 PMD 0   Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP   CPU: 20 UID: 1000 PID: 1272 Comm: nested_tdp_faul Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-8c89f11d1a99b-sink-vm #1914 PREEMPTLAZY   Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (Q35 + ICH9, 2009), BIOS 0.0.0 02/06/2015   RIP: 0010:nested_ept_get_eptp+0xb/0x10 [kvm_intel]   Call Trace:    <TASK>    kvm_mmu_load+0xcd/0x870 [kvm]    kvm_arch_vcpu_ioctl_run+0x18f5/0x1f80 [kvm]    kvm_vcpu_ioctl+0x2c7/0x970 [kvm]    __x64_sys_ioctl+0x90/0xd0    do_syscall_64+0x9c/0x4d0    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x4b/0x53   RIP: 0033:0x47491b    </TASK>   Modules linked in: kvm_intel kvm irqbypass   CR2: 0000000000000078   ---[ end trace 0000000000000000 ]---   RIP: 0010:nested_ept_get_eptp+0xb/0x10 [kvm_intel]  [sean: write changelog]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  KVM: SEV: Fix page dirtying in sev_gmem_post_populate()  set_page_dirty() requires that the caller holds some kind of lock to ensure that the page's mapping does not concurrently go away. That is not the case for a random page we got from get_user_pages_fast(), so use set_page_dirty_lock().  [sean: tag for stable]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  x86/kvm: Don't consume async #PF flags on a kernel #PF in NMI context  An async #PF "page not present" event arrives through the #PF vector, and its reason sits in the per-CPU apf_reason.flags until __kvm_handle_async_pf() reads and clears it. If an NMI arrives after the event is injected and before the #PF handler reads the flags, and the NMI handler itself takes a #PF, that fault reads and clears the flags belonging to the #PF it interrupted. It then finds interrupts disabled in the NMI context it interrupted, and panics:    Kernel panic - not syncing: Host injected async #PF in interrupt disabled region   Call Trace:    <NMI>    panic+0x52/0x60    __kvm_handle_async_pf+0xb0/0xb0    exc_page_fault+0x71/0xb0    asm_exc_page_fault+0x27/0x30   RIP: 0010:__get_user_nocheck_8+0x6/0x20    perf_callchain_user+0x147/0x1a0    get_perf_callchain+0x12d/0x1c0    ...    perf_event_nmi_handler+0x26/0x50    exc_nmi+0xe8/0x110   RIP: 0010:asm_exc_page_fault+0x0/0x30    </NMI>  The last RIP line shows the NMI landing on the first instruction of the #PF entry. perf with user call chains takes such a fault: the sampling NMI walks the user stack with __get_user(), which faults when a saved frame pointer is not a valid user address or the walk runs off the top of the stack. The same window exists when KVM, running as an L1 hypervisor with DELIVERY_AS_PF_VMEXIT, reads the flags itself after a #PF VM-exit.  The NMI entry code saves and restores CR2 for this nesting, but not the async #PF reason. Andy Lutomirski described the race, with perf as the example, when async #PF delivery was reworked in 2020 [1]. Saving and clearing the flags across the NMI, next to CR2, was discussed there but not merged.  Since that rework, Linux has stopped setting KVM_ASYNC_PF_SEND_ALWAYS, so the host delivers "page not present" only for user mode faults and a kernel-mode fault in NMI context (including kernel-mode #MC and #DB) cannot be an async page fault.  In that case, return without touching the flags so that the interrupted handler finds them intact.  Tested on v7.3-rc5 in a 4-vCPU, 2 GiB guest restored from a snapshot whose memory is served on demand through userfaultfd, so that reading it back takes async #PFs, while every thread samples hardware cycles with user call chains and points its frame pointer at an unmapped page. Without this patch the guest panicked as above in 3 of 3 runs. With it, the guest survived 3 of 3 runs of 60 seconds, and the host counted 148,441 to 153,334 kvm_async_pf_not_present events in the first 20 seconds of each. On 6.18.50 the results were the same: the guest panicked without the patch and survived with it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  watch_queue: Fix note pool publication race in watch_queue_set_size()  There is a race between watch_queue_set_size() and post_one_notification(). watch_queue_set_size() publishes wqueue->notes, notes_bitmap, nr_pages and nr_notes with plain stores, and post_one_notification() reads them with plain loads under a different lock, so nothing orders the four stores against the poster's loads: depending on the build, notes can be stored last (gcc 14 on x86-64 does this).  Since keyctl_watch_key() lets a watch attach to a queue before it is sized, post_one_notification() can already be running on another CPU at that moment: it reads nr_notes > 0, passes its bounds check, and then reads notes while it is still NULL, dereferencing notes[0].  An unprivileged user triggers this reliably by watching one of its own keys through a notification pipe and racing ioctl(IOC_WATCH_QUEUE_SET_SIZE) on that pipe against keyctl(KEYCTL_SETPERM) on the key from another CPU, triggering:    BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000000   RIP: 0010:post_one_notification.isra.0+0xa2/0x1e0   Call Trace:    __post_watch_notification+0x148/0x180    keyctl_setperm_key+0x119/0x130    do_syscall_64+0x108/0x4c0    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f   Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt  Fix this by publishing nr_notes last with smp_store_release(), and by reading it once with smp_load_acquire() in post_one_notification() before the bitmap and the page array are touched.  A poster that observes a non-zero nr_notes then also observes the pool behind it; one that observes zero drops the notification as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  unicode: free the map after a grace period  generic_ci_d_hash() and generic_ci_d_compare() read sb->s_encoding and dereference the unicode map while a pathwalk in rcu mode holds nothing but rcu_read_lock(). The filesystems that use them, ext4, f2fs and tmpfs, drop the map with utf8_unload() from ->put_super(), which runs when the last reference to the mount goes away. A lookup that is still inside such a filesystem at that point reads a freed map.  With a pathwalk held up in utf8_casefold_hash() while the last reference to a casefolded tmpfs goes away:    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in utf8nlookup+0x74c/0x950   Read of size 8 at addr ff110001030fe658 by task walker/98   Call Trace:    <TASK>    utf8nlookup+0x74c/0x950    utf8byte+0x160/0x1560    utf8_casefold_hash+0x167/0x230    generic_ci_d_hash+0xdd/0x1c0    link_path_walk+0x11ad/0x1d30    path_lookupat+0x63/0xb00    filename_lookup+0x1f1/0x5b0    vfs_statx+0xd7/0x3b0   [...]   Allocated by task 94:    __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x249/0x560    utf8_load+0x4e/0x570    shmem_parse_opt_casefold.isra.0+0x92/0x270   [...]   Freed by task 97:    kfree+0x1db/0x5b0    shmem_put_super+0x72/0x170    generic_shutdown_super+0x14c/0x530    kill_anon_super+0x3a/0x60    deactivate_locked_super+0x9c/0xf0    cleanup_mnt+0x9f/0x130  So far that has been hard to hit. umount(2) waits for a grace period in namespace_unlock() before it drops the mount, so only a mount whose last reference goes away elsewhere, like the close of a file or a chdir out of a lazily unmounted directory, can race a walker. So it is reachable.  Delay the free until a grace period has passed. The map and the data table it holds a reference to then outlive any pathwalk that found the superblock before the mount went away. The reference on the data table module is dropped from the rcu callback as well. utf8-core is built in whenever CONFIG_UNICODE is set, so there is no module exit that would have to wait for the callbacks.  Overlayfs points the s_encoding of an overlay at the map of its first layer without taking a reference of its own. That stays correct. The layer is held by the overlay, so its map is dropped only after the overlay is gone.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  autofs: ignore notification errors from a replaced pipe  autofs_notify_daemon() takes a reference to the current notification pipe under wq_mutex, then drops the mutex before writing the request. The write can block while the daemon enters catatonic mode and installs a replacement pipe.  If the old pipe's reader is then closed, the delayed write returns -EPIPE and the generic error path enters catatonic mode again. That transition acts on the current superblock state, closes the replacement pipe, and releases the new daemon generation's wait queues.  Only enter catatonic mode when the pipe which failed is still the current pipe. Factor the already-locked transition so the identity check and state change are atomic with respect to another replacement.  This was reproduced on v7.3-rc5-337-gff47652a4b66c in a local QEMU guest. An unprivileged UID 65534 lookup filled the old packet pipe before a normal CATATONIC/SETPIPEFD restart. On the unmodified kernel, the new pipe received HUP and both a pending victim lookup and a later lookup failed with ENOENT in two out of two fresh-mount runs.  With this change, the new pipe remained active, received an intact 304-byte request, and both victim lookups completed in two out of two runs. Normal lookup and restart-without-a-blocked-writer controls passed. No KASAN, oops, refcount, or lock diagnostic was observed. A source reproducer and complete local logs are available privately on request.  The demonstrated impact is limited to denial of a shared autofs service during a legitimate daemon restart. No memory corruption, information leak, privilege escalation, or code execution primitive was observed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ASoC: SOF: ipc4-topology: Fix shift-out-of-bounds for aggregated ALH capture  When ch_count is smaller than blob->alh_cfg.device_count (e.g. a mono capture stream, such as a SmartMic, aggregated across multiple SDW links), step = ch_count / blob->alh_cfg.device_count truncates to 0. The subsequent GENMASK(step - 1, 0) then underflows step - 1 (u32) to UINT_MAX, causing GENMASK()'s internal shift to use an out-of-bounds exponent:    UBSAN: shift-out-of-bounds in sound/soc/sof/ipc4-topology.c:2363:13   shift exponent 18446744069414584384 is too large for 64-bit type 'long unsigned int'  Treat ch_count < device_count the same way as the existing "channels equal to output reference channels" case: apply the same ch_mask to every aggregated device instead of trying to split channels that can't be evenly divided.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  accel/rocket: search every core slot when looking up a scheduler  sched_to_core() walks rdev->cores[] up to rdev->num_cores, and rocket_remove() decrements num_cores for every core it removes. Unbind a core that is not the last one and the cores behind it fall outside the search, so sched_to_core() returns NULL for a core that is still bound and still running jobs. Neither caller checks the result:    rocket_job_run():      rocket_fence_create(core), core->dev   rocket_job_timedout(): dev_err(core->dev, "NPU job timed out")  Unbinding the middle core of the three on an RK3588 while three clients are submitting to all of them faults twice, once from the surviving core's job queue and once from its reset work:    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000220-0x0000000000000227]   Workqueue: fdad0000.npu drm_sched_run_job_work [gpu_sched]   pc : rocket_job_run+0x234/0x838 [rocket]   Call trace:    rocket_job_run+0x234/0x838 [rocket]    drm_sched_run_job_work+0x2cc/0xad8 [gpu_sched]    process_one_work+0x640/0x14f0    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]   Workqueue: rocket-reset-2 drm_sched_job_timedout [gpu_sched]   pc : rocket_job_timedout+0xf0/0x1e0 [rocket]   Call trace:    rocket_job_timedout+0xf0/0x1e0 [rocket]    drm_sched_job_timedout+0x188/0x6a0 [gpu_sched]  Both are the third core: the workqueue names are its device and its core->index, and it was left at slot 2 while num_cores had dropped to 2.  Search all the slots that were allocated, the way find_core_for_dev() now does. A core that is still bound is then found, and the two callers get the pointer they already assume they have.  This does not make unbinding one core out of several safe. An open client keeps an entity pointing at the scheduler of the core that went away: drm_sched reports it as not ready for every job that lands on it, and the client waits in dma_fence_default_wait for a fence that will never signal. Stopping the NULL dereference is what belongs in a fix; the rest wants more thought.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  accel/rocket: search every core slot when a core is removed  rocket_remove() decrements rdev->num_cores for each core it removes, while find_core_for_dev() searches slots 0 to num_cores - 1. Unbinding the cores in the order they were bound therefore loses the last one: by the time it is removed the search range has already shrunk past its slot, so find_core_for_dev() returns -1 and rocket_remove() gives up without doing anything.  num_cores never reaches zero, rocket_device_fini() never runs, and the file-scoped rdev keeps pointing at a device that is going away. Binding the cores again starts from that stale count, because rocket_probe() takes rdev->num_cores as the slot to fill. On an RK3588, which describes three cores, the second round lands on slots 1, 2 and 3 while rdev->cores was allocated with room for three:    rocket fdab0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 1 version: 1179210309   rocket fdac0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 2 version: 1179210309   rocket fdad0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 3 version: 1179210309  The write to rdev->cores[3] is past the end of the array.  Nothing in tree reads the core array often enough to notice, so the overrun is silent today. It turned up while testing a devfreq series on top of this, where a worker walks every core a few times a second, and UBSAN caught the first bool it read out of the overrun entry:    UBSAN: invalid-load in drivers/accel/rocket/rocket_devfreq.c:47:10   load of value 5 is not a valid value for type '_Bool'   Workqueue: devfreq_wq devfreq_monitor  Record how many slots were allocated and search all of them. Every core is then found on removal, num_cores reaches zero, the device is torn down and a later bind starts from a clean rdev.  This does not make unbinding a single core out of several work. probe still takes num_cores as the slot to fill, so rebinding one core while its siblings stay bound would write over a slot that is already in use, and rocket_open() still reaches for cores[0] whether or not anything is there. Both of those want more thought than a fix should carry.  Found by unbinding and rebinding all three cores on an Orange Pi 5 Plus. With this applied, 25 unbind/rebind rounds and 5 module unload/reload rounds run clean there: the cores land in slots 0, 1 and 2 every time, whichever order they are bound in, and the shared supply goes back to a single user after each round.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  firewire: core: fix race condition in split transaction handling  For a split transaction, either fw_core_handle_response() or split_transaction_timeout_callback() may manipulate the same transaction entry in the pending transaction list. The return value of timer_delete() is used to determine which function handles the entry. If the transaction is a split transaction and timer_delete() returns zero, the timeout callback may already be running. In this case, the response handler must leave the entry in the list for the timeout callback to remove.  A previous code refactoring broke this behavior, introducing a race condition in which both functions could process the same transaction. This could lead to a use-after-free on the transaction initiator side.  Fix the regression by ensuring that the response handler does not process the transaction when timer_delete() returns zero. The timeout callback is responsible for removing the entry from the pending transaction list.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  x86/insn-eval: Fix shadowed segment index in get_seg_reg_override_idx()  Commit 45e1dccc0653 ("x86/insn: Simplify for_each_insn_prefix()") made for_each_insn_prefix() declare its own loop counter named idx. get_seg_reg_override_idx() keeps its result in a local of the same name, so the assignments in the loop body now write the loop counter:   - the function always returns INAT_SEG_REG_DEFAULT, so FS and GS    overrides are ignored;   - a CS override sets the counter to INAT_SEG_REG_CS (2), the increment    makes it 3, and prefixes.bytes[3] holds the last prefix, 0x2e again,    so the loop never terminates.  The UMIP emulation reaches this from the #GP handler for user space: an SGDT, SIDT or SMSW with a memory operand and a CS prefix leaves the task spinning in the kernel, never returning to user space, with a SIGKILL that is never delivered.  Any user can thus tie up CPUs until reboot. With an FS or GS prefix, the emulated result is written to the wrong address.  Rename the internal macro iterator variable.  [ Lukas' original patch renamed the use site, I changed it to rename the   iterator in the macro instead, but left Lukas' commit message and   authorship   - Linus ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  perf: Fix perf_pmu_migrate_context() leaving events behind  __perf_pmu_remove() walks the group leaders of a CPU and PMU with perf_event_groups_for_cpu_pmu(), removing each one as it goes. perf_remove_from_context() takes the leader out of the groups rbtree, after which rb_next() on that node returns NULL, prematurely ending the walk. Other groups stay behind in the source context.  On CPU hotplug, they are then torn down with the dying CPU. They keep running until teardown, while the PMU's interrupt and migrated events are on a new CPU, which drivers rely on never happening.  Walk ctx->event_list instead and pick out the PMU's events by their pmu_ctx.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: stmmac: dwmac1000: clear the RGMII status interrupt  Since commit 2e2c878a3141 ("net: stmmac: remove SGMII/RGMII/SMII interrupt handling") nothing on the RGMII path reads GMAC_RGSMIIIS, so RGSMIIIS stays pending behind GMAC_INT_MASK from the first link change on. stmmac_resume() resets the MAC in stmmac_hw_setup(); the reset sets GMAC_INT_MASK to 0 until dwmac1000_core_init() writes the mask again, and the pending status storms the line:    dwmac_dma_interrupt: unexpected status 04000000  A register dump at the first message on ODROID-HC4 showed it:    core int_status 00000001 int_mask 00000000 pmt 00000000 rgsmiiis 0000000d  When the resume thread runs on the CPU that takes the MAC interrupt, the storm starves it: a soft lockup, then a watchdog reset or a hang.  Read GMAC_RGSMIIIS in dwmac1000_irq_status() when the status is not masked, as the driver did before 2e2c878a3141; the read clears it.  Wake-on-LAN resume from s2idle with the resume thread and the MAC interrupt on one CPU: Helios64 (dwmac-rk), 7.3-rc6, soft-locked in 3 of 3 resumes without a fix and in 0 of 10 with this patch; it ran with an out-of-tree dwmac-rk change that keeps the GMAC powered across suspend. ODROID-HC4 (dwmac-meson8b): 0 of 10 with this patch, 2 of 2 without a fix on a 7.3-rc5 build. irq_rgmii_n went up by one per resume.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  gpio: mxc: fix race between chained IRQ handler install and probe completion  mxc_update_irq_chained_handler() is called before the IRQ domain, the generic IRQ chip, and the port list entry are set up. If an interrupt arrives in that window:   - mx3_gpio_irq_handler() calls generic_handle_domain_irq() with    port->domain still NULL.  - mx2_gpio_irq_handler() walks mxc_gpio_ports, but the port has not    been added to the list yet.  Additionally, if any of the subsequent probe steps (gpio_generic_chip_init(), devm_gpiochip_add_data(), irq_domain_create_legacy(), or mxc_gpio_init_gc()) fail, the error paths never unregister the chained handler, leaving a dangling handler that points at freed memory.  Move the handler installation after all its dependencies are ready and after list_add_tail(), so the handler is never live while the data structures it touches are incomplete, and is never installed if probe fails.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  gpiolib: fix memory leak in gpiod_set_array_value_complex() on error paths  A drive-by review by Sashiko reports that, after a failed call to gpiochip_set_multiple(), gpiod_set_array_value() returns abruptly, bypassing the freeing of possibly alloced bitmaps, potentially leaking memory. It is an unlikely error path, but is possible.  Defer the return code check until after the bitmap_free() block.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  calipso: keep BIG TCP payload_len in calipso_skbuff_setattr()  calipso_skbuff_setattr() adjusts payload_len by the length of the option it inserts or resizes:  	payload = ntohs(ip6_hdr->payload_len); 	ip6_hdr->payload_len = htons(payload + len_delta);  GRO can build BIG TCP packets larger than IPV6_MAXPLEN, and stores payload_len == 0 for them; ipv6_payload_len() then falls back to skb->len.  For such a packet forwarded to a destination mapped to CALIPSO, the code above writes len_delta (or 65536 + len_delta when shrinking) into payload_len, and ipv6_payload_len() no longer falls back to skb->len.  nf_tables, conntrack and sch_cake rely on it.  The same arithmetic also wraps when a packet grows past IPV6_MAXPLEN, and a BIG TCP packet that shrinks below IPV6_MAXPLEN should get its real length back.  Set payload_len from the skb length with ipv6_set_payload_len(), which stores 0 above IPV6_MAXPLEN and the real length otherwise, as ipv6_gro_complete() does.  The network header was just reset to skb->data, so skb->len - sizeof(*ip6_hdr) is the payload length.  Tested on one kernel (arm64, QEMU) with SELinux permissive, a minimal mdp-generated policy (network_peer_controls=1), "netlabelctl calipso add pass doi:16" and a NetLabel mapping of fd00:2::/64 to CALIPSO DOI 16.  calipso_skbuff_setattr() was called through netlbl_skbuff_setattr() from a test-only debugfs hook (not part of this patch) adding a level-only label; payload_len after the call:    case                         before fix   after fix   real length   1000, unlabeled                    1016        1016          1016   70000 GSO, payload_len 0             16           0         70016   65530 GSO, grows past MAXPLEN        10           0         65546   65540 GSO with a 24 byte hop   header, shrinks below MAXPLEN     65528       65532         65532   1000 with a 24 byte hop header      992         992           992  (0 means ipv6_payload_len() returns the real length.)  On the forward path, with a client injecting unlabeled UDP through a router to a server, the router adds the CALIPSO option and the server delivers all datagrams (Udp6InDatagrams 5, Ip6InTruncatedPkts 0) with this patch.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: bcmgenet: unshare the skb before writing the control block  bcmgenet stores first_cb, last_cb and bytes_sent in the skb control block and reads them back on completion to free the skb and credit BQL. ether_setup() leaves IFF_TX_SKB_SHARING set, so the stack can resubmit a shared skb that is still in the ring. The next transmit overwrites last_cb, so the earlier slots complete without crediting their bytes and BQL stalls the queue until the watchdog resets it.  Unshare the skb before writing the control block.  Reproduce with pktgen in clone_skb mode, which hands the driver the same skb while earlier copies are still in the ring:    modprobe pktgen   pg=/proc/net/pktgen   echo "add_device eth0" > $pg/kpktgend_0   echo "dst_mac AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF" > $pg/eth0   echo "dst 192.0.2.1" > $pg/eth0   echo "clone_skb 8" > $pg/eth0   echo "count 0" > $pg/eth0   echo start > $pg/pgctrl &   sleep 5   echo stop > $pg/pgctrl   wait   cat /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/tx-0/byte_queue_limits/inflight  inflight stays nonzero on the now idle queue. clone_skb 0 leaves it at zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: ti: icssm-prueth: Move setting of netops to fix crash  icssm_prueth_netdev_init() calls of_phy_get_and_connect() before ndev->netdev_ops is assigned. phy_attach_direct() -> phy_link_topo_add_phy() reads dev->netdev_ops through netdev_need_ops_lock() since the commit in question, so probing crashes with a NULL pointer dereference when CONFIG_NET_SHAPER is enabled.  Assign netdev_ops before the PHY attach, as was done for emac in commit 7c9f391ec89c ("net: emac: move setting of netops to fix crash").

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: ethernet: aeroflex: move setting of netops to fix crash  greth_of_probe() calls greth_mdio_init(), which connects the PHY, before dev->netdev_ops is assigned. phy_attach_direct() -> phy_link_topo_add_phy() reads dev->netdev_ops through netdev_need_ops_lock() since the commit in question, so probing crashes with a NULL pointer dereference when CONFIG_NET_SHAPER is enabled.  Assign netdev_ops before the PHY attach, as was done for emac in commit 7c9f391ec89c ("net: emac: move setting of netops to fix crash").

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net: ethoc: move setting of netops to fix crash  ethoc_probe() calls ethoc_mdio_probe(), which connects the PHY, before netdev->netdev_ops is assigned. phy_attach_direct() -> phy_link_topo_add_phy() reads dev->netdev_ops through netdev_need_ops_lock() since the commit in question, so probing crashes with a NULL pointer dereference when CONFIG_NET_SHAPER is enabled. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  netlink: avoid hashing the network namespace pointer  The netlink rhashtable key includes a raw struct net pointer and a user-controlled port ID. Both /proc/net/netlink and socket diagnostics expose the table's bucket order. By binding and rebinding chosen NETLINK_USERSOCK port IDs, an unprivileged reader can distinguish equal buckets and recover the low bits of the Jenkins hash. Its 32-bit seed and the limited set of kernel-image slides can then be searched offline to recover the address of init_net.  Use the namespace's unique, non-address net_cookie in the comparison key instead. It is assigned before the per-net initializers run and remains unchanged for the namespace's lifetime. The lookup key and object hash are still built by netlink_compare_arg_init(), keeping lookup, insertion, removal and rehashing consistent while preserving namespace separation. Neither public table walker needs to change.  Reading the socket's namespace cookie in netlink_compare() is safe under RCU, including during namespace teardown. netlink_release() removes the socket from the hash table and defers its final put with call_rcu(). cleanup_net() runs the per-net exit methods and waits for outstanding RCU callbacks with rcu_barrier() before freeing namespace storage.  Unlike ns.ns_id, net_cookie is also available and initialized during setup_net() in older stable kernels, making the change straightforward to backport to v5.15 and later.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: libsas: Fix SMP IO deadlock during HA resume  smp_execute_task_sg() calls pm_runtime_get_sync() on the host before issuing an SMP command. When that command is itself issued from the HA resume path, the get_sync() deadlocks: it waits for the ongoing resume (the device is RPM_RESUMING), while the resume is blocked in sas_drain_work() waiting for that same SMP IO to complete.  The deadlock needs an expander-attached SATA disk. During sas_resume_ha() -> sas_drain_work(), DISCE_RESUME -> sas_resume_sata() -> ata_sas_port_resume() requests ATA_EH_RESET, and the hard reset for such a disk is done via SMP PHY CONTROL (sas_ata_hard_reset() -> sas_phy_reset() -> sas_smp_phy_control() -> smp_execute_task_sg()). Direct-attached SATA resets through lldd_control_phy() and SSP devices use TMFs, so neither hits this.  Replace the get_sync()/put_sync() pair with pm_runtime_get_noresume()/pm_runtime_put(). smp_execute_task_sg() only needs to hold off autosuspend while the SMP is in flight, and it must not try to resume the host: a sync resume issued from the HA resume path itself is what deadlocks, and by the time sas_resume_ha() runs, hw_init has already reinitialized the hardware, so the device is accessible without one.  The usage reference is still required. Discovery work normally runs inside an event worker's PM reference, taken at sas_notify_port_event() notify time and held until the handler has flushed the disco queue. sas_rediscover_ex_phy() however requeues DISCE_REVALIDATE_DOMAIN from within the revalidation worker itself, and flush_workqueue() does not wait for work items queued during execution, so that chained revalidation runs with no outer PM reference - without the get_noresume(), its SMP could race autosuspend.  For the BSG path, sas_smp_handler() is the only caller which may find the host autosuspended: expander SMP requests do not go through any SCSI device request queue, so nothing else in that path holds the host awake. Resume it there with pm_runtime_resume_and_get() and check the result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  pipe: preserve existing fasync readers on writer setup failure  F_SETFL and FIOASYNC decide whether to invoke ->fasync() before pipe_fasync() takes pipe->mutex. Two enables of one O_RDWR FIFO can therefore both enter the callback.  fasync_helper() allocates before checking for an existing entry. If the first enable installs both entries, a second enable can update the reader entry and then fail the allocation for the writer entry. The error path removes the pre-existing reader entry, clearing FASYNC while the writer entry remains registered. __fput() then skips ->fasync(), so a later pipe notification can dereference the freed file or its f_owner. An unprivileged memory-pressure reproducer triggers a KASAN slab-use-after-free in send_sigio() through this path.  Keep the reader helper's result and undo the registration only if this call added it. The pipe mutex serializes changes to both lists, so a failed new registration still removes its reader, while a failed duplicate preserves the existing registrations and FASYNC. Successful duplicate enables continue to update fa_fd as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  ocfs2/dlm: Protect the recovery list during debugfs reads  Recovery participant records must remain alive while debug_state_print() walks reco.node_data and formats their fields. The formatter holds dlm->spinlock, but the recovery participant list is protected by dlm_reco_state_lock. In particular, dlm_destroy_recovery_area() detaches the list under dlm_reco_state_lock and frees the detached records after releasing it. A concurrent debugfs open can therefore read freed memory.  Protect the participant traversal and field reads in debug_state_print() with dlm_reco_state_lock, matching the existing list writers. This also serializes the traversal against list_add_tail() during recovery-area initialization. Make the existing lock available to the debug code through dlmcommon.h; the lock remains internal to the OCFS2 DLM module.  Release dlm->spinlock after formatting the other domain state and before acquiring dlm_reco_state_lock, so the debug reader does not nest the two locks. Leave recovery list insertion, detachment and freeing unchanged. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  sched/core: Call wakeup_preempt() for queued tasks during class change  Paul reported recent RCU changes exposed a lost resched where CPU idles with a rcutorture thread waiting while being completely runnable.  Dumping the rq state at the time of idling with runnable tasks showed the following:    rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class   rq->nr_running = 1   rq->cfs.h_nr_queued = 0   rq->rt.rt_nr_running = 1  Although the waiting task was an RT task, "rq->next_class" did not point to rt_sched_class and was stuck at the lower priority fair_sched_class.  Inspecting sched_change_end() revealed the following race with __sched_setscheduler() for queued, but non-running tasks:      CPU0                                   CPU1     ====                                   ====    __schedule()      /*      * rq->donor is a fair task that blocks.      * rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class      */      rq_lock(rq0)      pick_next_task()       /* nr_running = 0 */       pick_task_fair()         sched_balance_newidle()           raw_spin_rq_unlock(rq0)                                     rq_lock(rq0)                                      activate_task(rq0, p)                                       /* p is a fair task */                                       rq0->nr_running++;                                       rq0->cfs.h_nr_queued++;                                       wakeup_preempt(rq, p)                                         rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class                                         resched_curr()                                      rq_unlock(rq0)                                      __sched_setscheduler(p)                                       /* p is moved to SCHED_RR */                                       task_rq_lock(p)                                       sched_change_begin()  				      rq0->cfs.h_nr_queued--; 				      rq0->rt.rt_nr_running++;                                        sched_change_end()                                         /*                                          * p->on_rq = 1 (ctx->queued)                                          * but p is not rq->donor                                          * (!ctx->running) hence                                          * resched_curr() is and                                          * rq->next_class upgrade is                                          * skipped.                                          */                                         task_rq_unlock()            raw_spin_rq_lock(rq0)            /*            * rq->nr_running = 1            * rq->cfs.h_nr_queued = 0            * rq->rt.rt_nr_running = 1            * rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class            */             if (rq->cfs.h_nr_queued && ...)              /* Above is false */             if (rq_modified_above(this_rq, &fair_sched_class))              /* Also false since rq->next_class is still fair */        /*        * sched_balance_newidle() is considered to        * have failed to pull any fair tasks and no        * other wakeups were detected.        */        return NULL; /* pick_task_fair() */      pick_task_idle()       return rq->idle;      next = rq->idle;      /* Preemption indicators are lost */     clear_tsk_need_resched(prev);     clear_preempt_need_resched();      rq->curr = rq->idle;    !!! rq->idle switches in with rq->running == 1 but !need_resched() !!!  In simple words, enqueue, followed by a class change of the newly queued task goes unnoticed in rq->next_class indicator and sched_balance_newidle() sees no fair task, nor any higher priority task enqueued.  The above sequence will lead to CPU idling with a runnable task on the CPU.  Call wakeup_preempt() for ctx->queued cases in sched_change_end() to re-evaluate rq->next_class after class change (ENQUEUE_CLASS) and set the NEED_RESCHED indicator accordingly.  Newidle balance will correctly see an enqueue of a higher priority t ---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  scsi: target: Disable interrupts while holding delayed_cmd_lock  target_do_delayed_work() takes dev->delayed_cmd_lock with a plain spin_lock(). It runs from system_percpu_wq, so interrupts stay enabled while the lock is held. Every other acquisition of that lock uses spin_lock_irqsave(): target_handle_task_attr() and transport_complete_ordered_sync() in target_core_transport.c, and target_non_ordered_release() in target_core_device.c.  That was safe while every caller of transport_complete_task_attr() ran in process context: target_complete_ok_work() from target_completion_wq, transport_complete_qf() from dev->qf_work_queue, and transport_generic_request_failure() from the submit and execute paths.  Since commit 06933066d88a ("scsi: target: Add support for completing commands from backend context") that is no longer true. With complete_type=1 on a fabric that sets direct_compl_supp, target_complete() runs target_complete_ok_work() inline in the backend's completion context, which target_complete_cmd_with_sense() documents as "May be called from interrupt context". For iblock that is the bio end_io.  target_complete_ok_work() starts with transport_complete_task_attr(), which takes delayed_cmd_lock in two ways:   - Every ORDERED command is put on dev->delayed_cmd_list by    target_handle_task_attr() and dispatched from there by    target_do_delayed_work(), which marks it SCF_TASK_ORDERED_SYNC.  Its    completion therefore goes through transport_complete_ordered_sync().   - A SIMPLE command that completes while an ORDERED command is pending    drops the last reference to the killed dev->non_ordered, and    percpu_ref_put() then runs target_non_ordered_release() in the    completing context.  Both take the lock and, if commands are waiting, call schedule_work(&dev->delayed_cmd_work), which queues on system_percpu_wq, i.e. on the CPU that took the completion. Further completions for the same queue are typically delivered there too, so one arriving while the work holds the lock spins on it forever.  Reaching this needs complete_type=1, which is not the default (vhost-scsi, the only fabric with direct_compl_supp, defaults to TARGET_QUEUE_COMPL), a backend whose I/O completes from interrupt context, and ORDERED commands from the initiator. Linux virtio_scsi guests send only VIRTIO_SCSI_S_SIMPLE and never take the ordered path; any guest that uses the ORDERED task attribute, which vhost-scsi accepts, does.  target_do_delayed_work() is a work item and always runs in process context, so spin_lock_irq() is sufficient.  Found by inspection; no runtime report. A single ORDERED command goes through both acquisitions, so with CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING the first one completed through direct completion should produce an inconsistent lock state report on delayed_cmd_lock (hardirq or softirq, depending on where the backend completes).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  drm/xe/oa: Zero OA buffer at allocation  ttm_bo_type_kernel BOs are not guaranteed to be zeroed on allocation and may contain data from previously freed pages. Since the OA buffer is mmap'able by userspace, this can expose stale kernel memory contents.  Streams opened with DRM_XE_OA_PROPERTY_OA_DISABLED allocate the OA buffer without calling xe_oa_init_oa_buffer(). Zero the buffer at allocation to prevent information disclosure through mmap.  The existing zeroing in xe_oa_init_oa_buffer() remains necessary for zero report-id/timestamp detection on enable/re-enable.  (cherry picked from commit 126c4c5388f9311a390b9b254a835b0cf0f55331)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  drm/xe: skip eviction of a BO with no resource  xe_evict_flags() switches on tbo->resource->mem_type to choose an eviction placement. An xe BO can reach eviction with no ttm.resource, e.g. an imported dma-buf BO whose resource was freed during teardown while its attachment is still live: the exporter then invalidates it via xe_dma_buf_move_notify() -> xe_bo_evict(), and the switch dereferences a NULL resource and faults.  A BO with no resource has nothing placed or mapped, so there is nothing to evict. Return an empty placement (num_placement = 0), mirroring the handling already used for non-xe scatter-gather BOs just above; ttm_bo_validate() then takes the pipeline-gutting path and returns 0.  Without the fix the xe_dma_buf@xe_test_dmabuf_move_notify_no_resource dynamic live selftest will fail with below stack. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  accel/rocket: clear rdev on device init failure  rocket_probe() stores the return value from rocket_device_init() in the file-scoped rdev pointer before checking whether it is an error pointer. If rocket_device_init() fails, rdev is left as an ERR_PTR.  The rdev pointer is also used as the marker for whether the shared rocket device has already been initialized. A later core probe can therefore see a non-NULL rdev, skip rocket_device_init(), and dereference the error pointer when reading rdev->num_cores.  Save the error code and clear rdev before returning from the rocket_device_init() failure path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  netlink: reset skb headers before unicast and multicast filtering  Socket filters can use SKF_NET_OFF and SKF_LL_OFF to read relative to an skb's network and MAC headers. Netlink producers may reserve headroom without resetting those headers, allowing a receiving socket's filter to read data before the initialized message.  For example, IWPM HELLO replies are allocated with dev_alloc_skb(), which reserves NET_SKB_PAD bytes. An unprivileged NETLINK_RDMA user can attach a classic socket filter and disclose this headroom through the length of the delivered reply. The resets in netlink_dump() do not help because IWPM sends a separately allocated skb through netlink_unicast().  Reset both headers before running the receiver's filter in unicast and broadcast delivery, as is already done for dump skbs. This also covers other netlink producers that reserve headroom without changing their allocation or message-building code.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  net/rds: don't let the rdma_cm destroy an id RDS still owns on route failure  rds_rdma_cm_event_handler_cmn() hands the return value of rdma_resolve_route() straight back to the rdma_cm on RDMA_CM_EVENT_ADDR_RESOLVED.  A synchronous failure there - -ENOMEM from the route work allocation, an SA query that cannot be set up, a RoCE route with no usable device - makes addr_handler() destroy the id the event was delivered on.  That id is ic->i_cm_id, and nothing clears the pointer: the connection sits in RDS_CONN_CONNECTING with a freed id until its shutdown calls rdma_disconnect() and rdma_destroy_id() on it.  The ROUTE_RESOLVED case already avoids this: rds_ib_cm_initiate_connect() forces a zero return while ic->i_cm_id == cm_id, as the comment there explains.  Do the same here - drop the connection and return 0 - so the id stays RDS's to destroy from the shutdown, and the reconnect gets a fresh one.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  vsock: treat TCP_CLOSING as once-established  Handle the TCP_ESTABLISHED -> TCP_CLOSING transition on OP_RST, which can race with the connect loop. Immediately break and return 0 on ESTABLISHED/CLOSING. The return value of connect() should reflect what happened up to the point the connection was established or failed. Events that occur afterwards must not affect it. E.g. even if OP_RW has already set sk_err, connect() should still return 0, not ENOBUFS because of it. Adapt the inaccurate comment above signal_pending().  Resetting a socket that is still present in connected_table can lead to memory corruption. The reporter noted lost transports for in-flight skbs, and I have reproduced crashes caused by re-insertion into connected_table.    list_add double add: new=, prev=, next=.   kernel BUG at lib/list_debug.c:35!   Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI   Workqueue: vsock-loopback vsock_loopback_work   RIP: 0010:__list_add_valid_or_report+0x11f/0x130   Call Trace:    vsock_insert_connected.cold+0xe/0x13    virtio_transport_recv_pkt+0x10e9/0x1460    vsock_loopback_work+0x305/0x480    process_one_work+0xe4c/0x1560    worker_thread+0x4f1/0xd60    kthread+0x36e/0x470    ret_from_fork+0x47b/0x6b0    ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30  This fix is supplementary to commit 002541ef650b ("vsock: Ignore signal/timeout on connect() if already established"). In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  Drivers: hv: Don't reset VMBus connection state on error/exit paths  In two places, current code forces vmbus_connection.conn_state to DISCONNECTED prior to calling vmbus_disconnect(). But vmbus_disconnect() calls vmbus_initiate_unload(), which unloads the VMBus connection only if the conn_state is CONNECTED. Consequently, the connection remains and the Hyper-V host might continue to send messages or post VMBus interrupts.  The problem was introduced in commit 74347a99e73ae ("x86/Hyper-V: Unload vmbus channel in hv panic callback"), in that vmbus_initiate_unload() started checking the current connection state before doing the unload. This commit removed some occurrences where conn_state was forced to DISCONNECTED, but these two remained, apparently due to an oversight at the time.  Fix this by not forcing conn_state to DISCONNECTED during VMBus exit, or if a failure occurs when establishing the connection in the first place. Whatever value conn_state has at the time is then read by vmbus_initiate_unload() to determine if there is a connection to be unloaded.

Axel Download Accelerator 2.17.14 and earlier performs URL percent-decoding (http_decode()) on the output filename after the URL has been parsed and the filename component extracted. This allows an attacker to embed %2e%2e%2f (URL-encoded ../) sequences in the URL path. These sequences survive the URL parser intact (they contain no literal / characters) but are decoded into directory traversal sequences before the output file is opened for writing. As a result, a crafted URL can cause axel to write downloaded content to arbitrary filesystem paths relative to the current working directory.

Waline is a comment system with backend support. Prior to version 1.41.1, the login endpoint POST /api/token reads the email field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When email is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator. This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email. This issue has been patched in version 1.41.1.

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in the HTTP/2 request body reader of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust server memory via a request body sent as many 1-byte DATA frames.  do_read_data/5 in lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex keeps every DATA frame payload as its own list element until the read returns.
